questions.question: What is the difference between async and defer script attributes?
questions.title: Script Loading Async Defer
questions.direct_answer: Both download scripts in parallel without blocking HTML parsing — they differ in EXECUTION. async: executes as soon as it's downloaded, order NOT guaranteed — for independent scripts (analytics, pixel tags). defer: executes in document order after parsing completes, before DOMContentLoaded — for scripts that depend on each other or on the DOM (app code). Neither applies to inline scripts. Without either, a script blocks parsing until downloaded and executed.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Both download scripts in parallel without blocking HTML parsing — they differ in EXECUTION. async: executes as soon as it's downloaded, order NOT guaranteed — for independent scripts (analytics, pixel tags). defer: executes in document order after parsing completes, before DOMContentLoaded — for scripts that depend on each other or on the DOM (app code). Neither applies to inline scripts. Without either, a script blocks parsing until downloaded and executed.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The three loading modes, verified behavior:

```
<script src="app.js">
  HTML parser STOPS → download → execute → parser resumes
  Cost: nothing else happens while the script travels. The default = the worst.

<script async src="analytics.js">
  Download runs in parallel with parsing.
  The MOMENT it arrives, parsing pauses and it executes.
  ORDER: whatever finishes downloading first — NOT document order.
  Use: scripts with NO dependencies and nothing depending on them —
  analytics, A/B tags, pixels. Order-independent, fire-and-forget.

<script defer src="app.js">
  Download runs in parallel.
  Execution WAITS: runs in DOCUMENT ORDER, after parsing completes,
  right before DOMContentLoaded fires.
  Use: your app bundle — DOM ready + dependencies ordered + parse unblocked.
```

The decision rule (the interview answer):
- Does the script need the DOM? → defer (guaranteed parsed DOM at execution)
- Do multiple scripts depend on each other? → defer (order preserved)
- Fully independent, timing-irrelevant? → async (start it ASAP, don't care when)
- It's your main bundle in a modern build? → the build tool handles it (module scripts defer BY DEFAULT — <script type=module> never blocks the parser)

The DOMContentLoaded timing detail (the follow-up): deferred scripts run BEFORE DOMContentLoaded — listeners on that event can safely assume deferred scripts have run. Async scripts race it — an async script MAY execute after DOMContentLoaded (and after your app initialized — another reason async is only for independents).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph sync
        P1[parse] -->|stop| D1[download] --> E1[execute] --> P2[parse resumes]
    end
    subgraph async
        P3[parse...] -.parallel.-> D2[download]
        D2 -->|ready NOW| E2[execute — order = finish order]
    end
    subgraph defer
        P4[parse...] -.parallel.-> D3[download]
        P4 -->|parse done| E3[execute in ORDER] --> DC[DOMContentLoaded]
    end
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why the attributes exist at all (the history): pre-2008, every script was parser-blocking — pages with five scripts in <head> serialized five round-trips before rendering anything. async (IE-first, then standardized) and defer attacked the round-trip cost; the attribute pair is a 15-year-old performance API that's still the first lever on script-heavy pages.

The module-script default (the modern baseline): <script type=module> is deferred BY DEFAULT (and ESM is what bundlers emit). So modern apps mostly inherit defer semantics without writing it; the attribute pair matters mainly for third-party tags — the classic being an analytics snippet: async it (it must not delay your app), and a widget/embed that your code calls: defer or dynamic-import it AFTER your bundle loads (the sequencing bug: your code calls the widget's API before the widget's script executed — solved by loading order or onload-driven init).

The dynamic-loading layer (the programmatic tier): creating a script element and appending it = async by default; the pattern for loading third-party code ON DEMAND (a maps widget when the user opens the contact page). The heavy-hitter follow-up: every third-party tag you add is a main-thread cost — an async tag still EXECUTES on the main thread when it arrives (blocking whatever's rendering at that moment). The mitigation menu: load tags late (user-interaction-triggered for consent-gated analytics), use Partytown-style web-worker offloading for non-critical tags, and audit tags' execution cost like any other dependency — 'it's async' answers the download blocking, not the execution blocking.
